analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicaid nursing homes to pay nursing staff wages at least equal to the local average outside nursing homes.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a House vote: it sat in committee for 21 months, got one hearing, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Nursing aides and other nursing staff in nursing homes are among the lowest-paid health workers, and Medicaid pays the facilities that employ them. This bill would have required every nursing home that takes Medicaid to pay its nursing personnel — including aides — wages and benefits at least equal to the average paid to comparable nursing personnel working outside nursing homes in the same area. The requirement would have phased in over four years, states would have had to reimburse facilities for the part of the raise attributable to Medicaid patients, and states could claw back any of that money a facility did not actually spend on wages.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing personnel in nursing homes — especially nurses' aides, who are predominantly low-wage workers, many of them women — would gain a wage floor tied to what comparable workers earn elsewhere. Nursing home residents would also be positioned to benefit indirectly, since low pay drives high turnover and understaffing in facilities.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage nursing aides in nursing homes

how_it_helps.text: Requires nursing facilities participating in Medicaid to pay nursing personnel, including nurses' aides, at a rate at least equal to the mean rate paid to comparable nursing personnel employed outside nursing facilities in their locality [S2][S3].
Phases the requirement in over four years, starting at roughly two-thirds of the outside rate and reaching the full adjusted rate, so facilities have time to adjust [S2][S3].

Requires states to pay facilities for the wage and benefit costs attributable to Medicaid patients, and lets states recover through offset any of that money a facility receives but does not spend on nursing wages — a pass-through with teeth [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Nursing facilities would bear the cost of raising pay to the local average, enforced by state recovery of unspent funds. State and federal Medicaid budgets would cover the share of the raise attributable to Medicaid patients, meaning taxpayers pick up part of the bill. Facilities' non-Medicaid (private-pay) revenue would cover the rest.

drawbacks.text: The wage mandate raises facility operating costs, and the bill requires states to fund the Medicaid-attributable share, so federal and state Medicaid spending would rise — a real cost to taxpayers at a time when long-term care spending was already growing [S3].

A wage floor tied to the local mean could push up costs in a sector with thin margins; facilities might respond by cutting other staffing, pressing for Medicaid rate increases, or shifting costs to private-pay residents, none of which the bill directly addresses [S3].
The mandate applies only to nursing personnel covered by the wage surveys, not to other low-paid facility staff such as dietary or housekeeping workers, so the floor is narrow [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is straightforward: higher pay for very low-wage workers in exchange for higher Medicaid and facility costs. The bill's design tries to limit the burden — a four-year phase-in, state reimbursement of Medicaid-attributable costs, and clawback of funds not spent on wages — which addresses the common fear that money earmarked for wages gets absorbed elsewhere. The main unresolved risk is where non-Medicaid cost pressure lands: on private-pay residents, on other services, or on facility closures. It is a targeted intervention in a sector where low wages and turnover directly affect care quality, and the design is more careful than a blanket mandate.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its health subcommittee, which held a hearing in July 1990, but the committee never wrote it up or voted on it, and it expired when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Doug Walgren introduced the bill on March 23, 1989, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1][S5].
It gathered 48 cosponsors — 41 House Democrats and 7 House Republicans — a bipartisan group [S4].
On April 17, 1989, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, where it sat for over a year [S5].
The subcommittee held hearings on July 20, 1990, but the full committee never reported the bill, and no chamber ever voted on it before the Congress ended January 3, 1991 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing facility operators are better off: they never had to raise aides' pay to the local average or face clawback of Medicaid funds, and the Congress that could have mandated it adjourned without acting.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing facility operators, who avoided the wage mandate

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 48 cosponsors, including 41 of 257 House Democrats and 7 of 175 House Republicans — and the record shows no organized opposition vote; the bill simply never advanced out of committee [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Nursing homes and long-term care facilities
industries.note: The bill would have forced facilities that take Medicaid to pay nursing staff the local outside-facility average, with states recovering any earmarked wage funds a facility did not spend. Facilities had been able to pay below the outside rate; this would have ended that, with states covering the Medicaid-attributable share of the increase [S3].

States would have gained a tool to claw back Medicaid funds not spent on nursing wages, tying payments to actual worker pay — but they would also have had to absorb higher Medicaid payment costs for the mandated raises [S3].
